text: Germany's far-right AFD has just scored a historic election result. The first projections from Saxony-Anhalt put the AFD at around 44.5% of the vote, and this is particularly significant because the AFD's branch of Saxony-Anhalt has been officially classified by the state's domestic intelligence agency as confirmed right-wing extremist. Is a far-right party actually coming to power in Germany? Some of you may know that I currently live in Germany, and you may have seen the news that the AfD, a party routinely described by major media outlets as far-right and sometimes described by politicians and commentators as extremist, fascist, or even Nazi, just won an election with an absolutely massive result of almost 44%. And predictably, this sent shockwaves through German politics and quite a bit of panic through social media. If you only saw some of the headlines and TikToks, you could easily get an impression that AFD just won Germany. But that's not actually what happened. Germany is made up of 16 federal states, and each state has its own parliament and state government. This election was only for Saxony-Anhalt, a relatively small eastern German state with around 2.1 million people. It was not a national election, so AFD did not win Germany's national parliament, the Bundestag. They did not replace Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and they are not suddenly in charge of Germany's national immigration, foreign or economic policy. But here's where it gets interesting. They haven't even secured control of Saxony-Anhalt yet. The new state parliament has 83 seats. AFD won 39. An absolute majority requires 42. And that matters because voters don't directly elect the head of the state government. The parliament elects the minister-president, basically the prime minister of that state. So AFD came just three seats short of having enough lawmakers to elect their candidate and govern with a parliamentary majority completely on their own. Normally, this is where the biggest party finds another party and forms a coalition. That's also how Germany is currently governed nationally. CDU, CSU and SPD govern together because neither has enough seats alone. But AFD has a problem called the Brandmauer, or firewall. Basically, Germany's other major parties have spent years refusing to form government with AFD. In Saxony-Anhalt, CDU, SPD, Greens and the left have all rejected an AFD coalition. So you can win 44% of the vote, but winning the election does not automatically mean you get to govern. There is one particularly interesting party here, BSV. They have five seats. So mathematically, AFD's 39 plus BSV's 5 equals 44. Enough for a majority. But BSV has not agreed to join an AFD coalition. At least not at the moment of this recording. Its leadership says it doesn't want a formal coalition with AFD. What BSV does say is that it rejects the firewall and is willing to cooperate with AFD on individual issues. It has even discussed the possibility of an AFD minority government. That would mean AFD could run the state government without controlling a majority of parliaments, but it would then need support from other parties to pass laws and budgets. And there's another interesting twist. If nobody can elect a minister president with an absolute majority in the first two attempts, Saxony-Anhalt can eventually hold another vote with a lower threshold. A majority of the votes actually cast. So AFD's 39 votes could potentially become enough if some other lawmakers abstain or if the opposition cannot unite behind one candidate. So no, AFD has not taken over Germany. And at this point, it hasn't even definitely taken over Saxony-Anhalt. But this election is still a very big deal. AFD nearly doubled its previous support, came within three seats of an outright parliamentary majority, and could potentially produce Germany's first AFD-led state government. And state governments still have significant powers over things like schools, police-slash-law enforcement, and culture. And they also participate in federal politics through Germany's Bundesrat. But this election gives AFD zero additional seats in the national Bundestag. The next federal election, the big one, is still about two and a half years away, in spring 2029, when the whole country votes separately. So the accurate headline isn't the far right just took over Germany. It is more like AFD just achieved a historic landslide in one German state, came extremely close to governing it alone, and Germany is now finding out whether its political firewall can survive when almost 44% of voters choose the party it was designed to keep out of government.
